Infamous means widely known for something bad, evil, or morally wrong.

It has two ideas locked together inside it:

  • Known by many people (like being famous)
  • For something terrible (a crime, cruelty, disgrace, or evil)

So if someone or something is infamous, the world hasn't just heard of them — the world has heard of them specifically because of how bad they are.
The Key Idea: It's Not Just "Bad." It's "Famously Bad."

This is the most important thing to understand. There is a difference between:

  • A pickpocket on a street corner — they are bad, but nobody knows who they are.
  • A serial killer whose crimes shocked an entire nation for decades — they are infamous.

The pickpocket may be just as morally wrong, but infamous requires a reputation. The badness must have spread — people must know about it, talk about it, and remember it.

Think of it this way: infamous = famous + evil/disgrace.

The word can describe many kinds of things:

A person — A dictator who ordered mass killings. A corrupt politician whose crimes destroyed thousands of lives. A fraudster who robbed millions of people of their savings.

An event — A battle where thousands were slaughtered needlessly. A disaster caused by human negligence. A political scandal that brought down a government.

A place — A prison known for its brutal conditions. A location where a terrible historical atrocity took place.

An action or decision — A law that was deeply unjust. A speech full of hate. A military order that caused unnecessary civilian deaths.

Example sentences:

  • Al Capone was an infamous gangster who ran a violent criminal empire in Chicago.
  • The 1929 St. Valentine's Day Massacre was one of the most infamous events in American crime history.
  • The factory became infamous for its dangerous working conditions and multiple deaths.
  • He made an infamous decision to abandon his soldiers in the middle of battle.

Infamous is a strong word. It is not used for small, everyday wrongs. You wouldn't call someone infamous for lying about being sick to skip work, or for cutting in line at a grocery store. The badness attached to "infamous" is usually serious — it involves significant harm, deep moral failure, or widespread damage to others.

It often carries a tone of lasting judgment. When you call something infamous, you are saying that history itself has stamped it as wicked or disgraceful. It's the kind of word used for things that people don't easily forget or forgive.
How It Differs from Similar Words

Famous — Simply means widely known. It carries no moral judgment at all. A singer can be famous. A scientist can be famous. A kind doctor can be famous. Famous is neutral. Infamous is always negative.

Notorious — This is the closest word to infamous, and they are often used interchangeably. Both mean "widely known for something bad." However, notorious tends to focus on the fact of being widely known, while infamous tends to carry a slightly stronger sense of moral outrage or disgrace. In most everyday writing and speech, you can treat them as near-synonyms.

Evil / Wicked / Terrible — These words describe how bad something is, but they say nothing about whether people know about it. Infamous always includes the element of public knowledge or reputation.

Disreputable — This means having a bad reputation, but on a smaller or more personal scale. A disreputable business might just be dishonest in minor ways. Infamous is bigger — it implies the reputation is widespread and the wrongdoing is serious.
A Common Mistake to Watch Out For

Some people mistakenly use "infamous" to simply mean "very famous" — as if it were just a stronger version of "famous." This is incorrect.

❌ "She is infamous for her amazing singing voice."
✅ "She is famous for her amazing singing voice."

❌ "The restaurant is infamous for its delicious food."
✅ "The restaurant is famous for its delicious food."

Infamous must always be tied to something bad, shameful, or morally wrong. If what the person is known for is good, neutral, or admirable, you cannot use infamous.

When you read or hear the word "infamous," it should trigger a feeling of dark recognition — the sense that you're being reminded of something the world agreed was wrong, dangerous, or deeply shameful. It is a word that carries weight. Writers use it to signal that what follows is not just bad news, but a matter of serious moral or historical significance.
Infamous = well-known, but for all the wrong reasons.
